caption:
Dentist, glasses, pills: $2,000 this year? Claim them on one return, usually the lower earner's.

In Canada, one of you can claim the medical bills for both partners and your kids under 18, all together, on one tax return (line 33099).

WHY: only the part of the bills above a floor counts. The floor is 3% of the claimer's net income, or a fixed amount if that is less ($2,891 for 2026; $2,834 for 2025). A lower income means a lower floor, so more of the same bills count.

The maths (made up for this post): $2,000 of bills.
• You earn $90,000: 3% is $2,700, more than the bills, so $0 counts.
• Your partner earns $40,000: 3% is $1,200, so $800 counts for the credit.
That $800 is not money back. It's the amount the credit is worked out on: $800 x 14% = $112 off your federal tax for 2026, plus your province's own credit.

HOW:
1. Gather every receipt: dentist, prescription glasses, prescription drugs, and the rest of the CRA's list.
2. Pick any 12-month period that ends in the tax year.
3. In your tax app, enter the bills on the lower earner's return first, then check the other return too, and keep the one that cuts more tax.

THE CATCH: it's a non-refundable credit, so it only lowers tax the claimer owes. If the lower earner owes little or no tax, the other return may work better. Purely cosmetic work and over-the-counter medicine don't count. Keep the receipts.

WHO THIS IS FOR: you, your spouse or common-law partner, and your or their kids under 18. Bills for other relatives who depend on you (an adult child, a parent) go on line 33199, with their own rules.

Do this: Claim them on line 33099, usually on the lower earner's return. Check both in your tax app.

Send this to whoever does the taxes in your home.

Education only, not financial advice.

Follow for one money rule a day, in plain words.

first_comment:
Sources (checked Nov 4 2026; updated Nov 5 2026):
• CRA, 'Medical Expenses 2025' (RC4065, canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/forms-publications/publications/rc4065/medical-expenses.html, modified 2026-01-20): line 33099 covers eligible expenses 'you or your spouse or common-law partner paid' for you, your spouse or partner, and your or their children under 18; you claim the total minus the lesser of $2,834 or 3% of your net income (line 23600); any 12-month period ending in 2025. In its worked story, 'Either Richard or Pauline can claim this amount on line 33099', and the lower-income partner (Richard, $42,000) gets the bigger claim ($5,040 vs $4,650). Lists dental services, prescription eyeglasses and prescription drugs; excludes purely cosmetic procedures and over-the-counter medicine.
• Finance Canada, 'Report on the Impact of Reducing the Lowest Marginal Personal Income Tax Rate on Non-Refundable Tax Credits' (canada.ca): the rate for most non-refundable credits, including the medical expense credit, is based on the lowest personal income tax rate (14% in 2026). CRA 'Current year tax rates and income brackets (2026)': 14% on the first $58,523.
The $2,000 of bills and the $90,000 / $40,000 incomes are made up for this post; the maths is ours (3% of income).
• TaxTips.ca, 'Tax credits 2026' (taxtips.ca/nrcredits/tax-credits-2026.htm, checked Nov 5 2026): federal medical expense threshold $2,891 for 2026 (line 33099); federal credit rate 14%. (CRA's 2026 RC4065 isn't published yet; the 2025 amount, $2,834, is from CRA RC4065.)
The $112 is our maths: $800 x 14% (federal only, 2026).
